To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the concepts that we used during the initial encoding of ambiguous faces influenced facial EMG activity; (b) facial EMG activity during passive viewing of the faces predicted memory bias for the faces; (c) the concepts that participants encoded with the faces did not influence their memory for the faces; and (d) the facial EMG activity observed in the current study was not observed in the absence of emotional concepts or when participants encoded and viewed Chinese ideographs.

the facial EMG responses during the encoding of faces with emotion concepts are predictive of memory for the emotional expression of those faces, and that the spontaneous facial EMG responses to the faces during passive viewing is predictive of the subsequent memory for those faces.
(1) emotion concepts guide perception, (2) perception of facial expression guides facial action, and (3) facial action predicts memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the body in the development and expression of emotion, with the body understood as a dynamic, embodied, and enactive system that is inextricably linked to the world.
the relationship between the body and the mind, and how this relationship influences our perception of others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study by Kassam et al. (2010) provides a strong and well-controlled evidence for the role of embodiment in emotional processing.

the study of embodied simulation via EMG as participants first encoded emotion concepts and later passively viewing ambiguous faces without concepts, the results of the study showed that the participants showed more smiling-related EMGs activity in response to the faces paired with happy than in response to the face paired with angry, and later, in the absence to concept, the participants remembered the happy faces as happier than angry faces.

the results of the current study support the idea that embodied emotion simulation is a mechanism by which emotional concepts guide emotion perception and that this mechanism is specific to emotional concepts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
emotion concepts influence how people perceive and remember faces.
we found that when people think about emotions, they simulate them, and that the simulation is specific to the emotion that they are thinking about.
we show that the conceptually guided perception of facial emotion is associated with the activation of facial muscles that are typically used to display the perceived emotion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
emotion concepts guide perception and facial action in a way that is consistent with the embodiment framework.
emotion concepts can bias how we perceive and remember emotional faces.
the concepts we use to think about emotion guide our perception and memory of emotion.
